title: Selling Indian Property to Another NRI? The Buyer Must Still Deduct TDS — at 12.5% or More
excerpt: When an NRI sells property in India, the buyer must deduct tax at source under the non-resident rules no matter who the buyer is — there is no Rs 50 lakh threshold and no basic-exemption adjustment for the seller. A lower deduction certificate, obtained before the sale, is the main tool to stop excess tax being locked up until the return is filed.
body:
• When an NRI sells property in India, TDS must be deducted under the non-resident rules even if the buyer is another NRI — the duty follows the seller's status, not the buyer's, according to ICICI Bank's NRI guide.
  • For a property held more than 24 months, TDS runs at 12.5 percent plus surcharge and cess on the long-term gain basis; short-term holdings are taxed at the seller's applicable rates — far above the 1 percent resident rate.
  • There is no Rs 50 lakh threshold and no basic-exemption adjustment for an NRI seller, so even a small gain is fully taxable in India.
  • A Lower Deduction Certificate obtained before the sale is the practical fix: without one, excess TDS stays locked up until the seller files an Indian return and claims a refund.

A common misconception among non-resident Indians is that the familiar 1 percent TDS on property sales applies when they sell to each other. It does not. An NRI can sell residential or commercial property in India to a resident or to another NRI, OCI or PIO, and in every case the sale is subject to TDS under the non-resident provisions — Section 195 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, now carried into Section 393(2) of the Income Tax Act, 2025 — regardless of who the buyer is, ICICI Bank explains in its guide to TDS on NRI property sales.

The Rates, and Why They Bite

The applicable rate turns on the holding period. Property held for more than 24 months produces long-term capital gains, taxed at 12.5 percent before surcharge and cess; with those added, the effective rate rises with the seller's total Indian income. Property held for 24 months or less produces short-term gains taxed at the rates in force for that seller. Inherited or gifted property takes the previous owner's holding period into account.

Two resident comforts are missing. The Rs 50 lakh threshold below which no TDS is deducted applies only to resident sellers. And the basic exemption adjustment against long-term gains — available to resident individuals — is not available to non-residents, so an NRI seller's gain is taxable in full, even a gain of Rs 2 lakh.

The cash-flow problem is worse than the tax bill. TDS is commonly deducted on the gross consideration rather than the gain, so the amount withheld can substantially exceed the tax eventually due, as a guide to NRI property sales notes. The excess comes back only after the seller files an Indian tax return.

The Lower Deduction Certificate

The remedy is to apply before the sale, not after. A seller who expects the actual liability to be lower than the default TDS can register on the TRACES portal and apply to the Income Tax Assessing Officer for a Lower Deduction Certificate, disclosing the gain computation and supporting documents. With the certificate in hand, the buyer deducts at the lower rate and the seller keeps the cash.

The buyer should not treat this as the seller's problem. A buyer who fails to deduct can be declared an assessee in default, face interest and penalties for late deposit, and can be treated as the seller's representative assessee. Registration itself can stall when the TDS paperwork is incomplete.

Reducing the Final Bill, and Getting the Money Out

Two exemptions can cut the final tax on long-term gains: Section 54, for reinvesting the gain in another residential property in India within the prescribed timelines, and Section 54EC, for investing in notified bonds such as those of the National Highways Authority of India and the Rural Electrification Corporation, subject to their caps and lock-in.

Repatriation is a separate FEMA track. The seller can remit sale proceeds abroad — generally up to $1 million per financial year from rupee funds — once tax compliance is proved, with the bank requiring the sale deed and evidence of how the property was originally funded. Plan the TDS, the certificate, the return and the remittance together at the start of the transaction; handled in that order, an NRI-to-NRI sale is routine. Handled backwards, it is the refund and the stuck proceeds that everyone remembers.

This article is general information on the rules as published by the sources cited, not personal tax advice; individual cases turn on residence status, treaties and the property's history.
